The Antalya minnow, Pseudophoxinus antalyae, is a small cyprinid endemic to a few isolated freshwater springs in southwestern Turkey. Studies of growth patterns from wild-caught specimens indicate that the species attains a maximum recorded total length of 19 centimeters [Li = 19 centimeters], a modest size that is typical for members of the genus inhabiting resource-limited Mediterranean stream systems. Reproduction in this species is tightly linked to thermal conditions; controlled aquarium experiments have demonstrated that when maintained at a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], gravid females produce a maximum of approximately 4.93 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 4.93 eggs per day]. This relatively low fecundity is offset by an extended spawning season and likely reflects the energetic constraints of living in a thermally stable yet oligotrophic environment. The body size at which individuals first become reproductively active further corroborates the species’ slow life history, with puberty occurring at a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters]. This length is reached after a prolonged juvenile phase, during which the fish must accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis.

The initial biological investment in each offspring is remarkably small. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva possesses an average wet weight at birth of just 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], reflecting a diminutive egg size with a typical diameter near 1.5 millimeters. The lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the initial days following eclosion, when it remains largely immobile near the substrate. This period of endotrophic development is critical, as the tiny prolarva must absorb its yolk before transitioning to exogenous feeding on microcrustaceans and rotifers. The larval stage is characterized by rapid but metabolically efficient growth; by the time the swim bladder is fully inflated and the mouth is open for first prey capture, the body mass has already increased several-fold. The minuscule neonatal mass places a premium on the timing of hatch, which must synchronize with the spring bloom of zooplankton to ensure adequate first-feeding success. Field observations from the type locality indicate that newly emerged prolarvae are extremely vulnerable to siltation and rapid temperature fluctuations, factors that contribute to high early-life mortality.

As individuals progress through the exotrophic larval and juvenile stages, the allometric shift in body shape becomes pronounced, with the head and trunk elongating relative to the tail. Continued somatic growth eventually leads to an ultimate wet weight of 129 grams [Wwi = 129 grams] in the largest, most well-nourished adults. This asymptotic mass is attained only after several years of sustained feeding, and data from mark-recapture studies suggest that growth rate slows substantially once fish reach approximately two-thirds of their final body length. The species exhibits a classic indeterminate growth trajectory, with older males in particular continuing to add some mass even after reaching reproductive maturity, albeit at a greatly reduced annual increment. This maximum recorded adult body mass stands in contrast to that of many other Anatolian cyprinids, which often exceed 300 grams, and likely reflects the relatively low productivity of the groundwater-fed habitats to which Pseudophoxinus antalyae is confined. The relationship between length and weight follows a predictable power curve, allowing researchers to estimate condition factors from non-lethal length measurements during population surveys.

The transition from juvenile to adult is marked by a distinct reproductive milestone. At the onset of puberty, females typically attain a wet weight at puberty of 6.5 grams [Wwp = 6.5 grams], a body size that corresponds closely with the length threshold of 7 centimeters observed for gonadal maturation. At this mass, vitellogenesis begins and the ovaries develop the first cohort of maturing oocytes. The energetic cost of this reproductive activation is substantial; individuals below this weight threshold rarely show signs of gonadal recrudescence even if they are of adequate age, suggesting that a minimum energy reserve is required before the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is fully activated. Comparative data from congeneric species, such as Pseudophoxinus elizavetae, indicate that a similar size-based pubertal trigger is common across the genus, although the absolute mass at puberty can vary with local trophic conditions. In Antalya minnow, the 6.5 grams threshold represents roughly 5 percent of the ultimate adult mass, a ratio that aligns with the pattern observed in other small-bodied, iteroparous cyprinids that inhabit stable spring environments.

Maximum longevity under natural conditions has been estimated from scale annuli and otolith readings. At the same stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] that governs the species’ reproductive output, the oldest documented individuals have been recorded at a life span of 10 years [am = 10 years], though most wild fish likely do not survive past their eighth year. This extended lifespan, unusual for a fish of such small ultimate size, is a hallmark of a slow-paced life history strategy adapted to a low-mortality, resource-poor environment. The trade-off between early reproduction and survival is clearly evident: females that delay their first spawning until they have reached a larger body size tend to achieve higher lifetime fecundity, despite having fewer total reproductive seasons. Senescence becomes apparent after the seventh year, with declining body condition and reduced gamete quality noted in both sexes.
